newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Kidnapped Briton still in Khmer Rouge hands - premier.
newsitem.headline: Kidnapped Briton still in Khmer Rouge hands - premier.

text.p: Kidnapped Briton Christopher Howes remains in the hands of Khmer Rouge hard-liners loyal to Pol Pot, Cambodia's first prime minister said on Monday.
When asked if Howes was believed to be alive, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said: "He is with the Khmer Rouge. I really don't know."
On Saturday, a senior military official said the British mine clearance expert, held since last March, was alive and being held by a commander named Saroeun who supports Pol Pot.
The commander was with the hated Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot in jungle terrain after they fled the northern rebel stronghold of Anlong Veng with 250 to 300 troops, the official said.
"Mr Howes is with Mr Saroeun, who is with Pol Pot now," Ranariddh told reporters at a pagoda-opening ceremony in this village west of Phnom Penh.
On Saturday, Ranariddh's partner in power, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, said he thought Howes was dead.
Christopher Howes and his Cambodian translator, Houn Hourth, were abducted on March 26 last year while clearing mines in the northwest province of Siem Reap.
Authorities have said they were then taken to Anlong Veng, though the Khmer Rouge has consistently denied involvement in the attack.
Ranariddh said Khieu Samphan, president of the rebels' provisional government, had told him Howes was alive.
Most of Pol Pot's fighters deserted him on Sunday but the leader escaped with top figures towards the Thai border, Ranariddh said.
More than one million Cambodians died of starvation, execution, disease and hard labour during the Khmer Rouge rule from 1975-79.
The rebels, who reneged on a 1991 peace pact meant to end Cambodia's long conflict, have been fighting the coalition government formed following U.N. polls in 1993.
But the Khmer Rouge has been decimated by thousands of defections since last August, and before the recent split and fighting, fewer than 2,000 hard-line fighters were thought to remain.
